newsitem.title: USA: Texas abuse tape spurs unease over private prisons.
newsitem.headline: Texas abuse tape spurs unease over private prisons.

text.p: The videotaped abuse of convicts in southeast Texas has increased unease about using privately run facilities to ease overcrowding in U.S. prisons, criminologists said on Tuesday.

The dramatic tape -- which shows one howling inmate being bitten by a police dog and another being prodded with an electronic stun gun -- also raises the question whether states exporting inmates to private prisons are turning a blind eye to the potential for abuse, they said.

"I think we are going to see more of this as more and more states look for ways to offload their prison problems," said Timothy Flanagan, dean of the college of Criminal Justice at Sam Houston State in Huntsville, Texas.

The uproar began with the release this week of a "training video" showing guards in riot gear abusing several inmates during a drug search last September at the Brazoria County Detention Center in Angleton, Texas, about 25 miles south of Houston.

The guards said they made the training film to show "what not to do" to quell a prison uprising, but criminologists said it provided insight into the largely unregulated private prisons sprouting up nationwide.

"Abuses of prisoners, unfortunately, are not uncommon," University of Florida criminologist Charles Thomas said. "This is not the first time that there has been a problem involving Missouri prisoners down in Texas."

Capital Correctional Resources Inc., a central Texas company operating the Brazoria prison, has three facilities in the state housing inmates under contracts with Missouri and Oklahoma, prison officials said.

More than 400 Missouri prisoners are being transferred out of the CCRI-run Brazoria County center this week, and Oklahoma is moving about 560 of its inmates back to the state from a CCRI-run facility in Limestone County after uncovering other alleged abuses.

"We had some concerns about the quality-of-life issue and the use of pepper spray. There seemed to be an inordinate use of pepper spray," Jerry Massie, spokesman for the Oklahoma Department of Corrections, said of the decision to move the inmates home.

Lon Glenn, an assistant warden at the Brazoria facility, said CCRI, based in Groesbeck, Texas, expected to be cleared of alleged wrongdoing in a pending civil lawsuit filed by a former inmate and a separate FBI civil rights investigation of the fracas.
"We expect to be vindicated if and when this thing goes to court," he said.

In a booming business, small Texas towns have been financing construction of private prisons to house out-of-state inmates. The state has become one of the top importers of prison inmates from elsewhere in the country.
At an average of $40 per day per inmate, the sector is generating millions of dollars a year for private companies and an economic development boon as they hire local guards to staff the prisons.

There are about 1.7 million prison beds in the United States, and private companies operate about 85,000 beds in local, state and federal prisons. But the private companies are quickly building market share. They accounted for 20 percent of the 100,000 beds added last year.

Texas, Oklahoma, Arizona and Minnesota have become the nation's leading importers of inmates, while Virginia, North Carolina, Oregon, Idaho, Utah, Missouri and Oklahoma lead the list of exporters, Thomas said.

Flanagan said that to some extent, there was a buyer's market in incarceration. "If you can't do the job and do it in a way that is constitutionally permissible, then you're not going to get the business," he said.
